Who sets and collects property tax

The state sets the value, and your county or town turns it into a bill. SDAT assesses real property and certifies the assessments to counties and municipalities, and those governments apply their own rates.

The system covers more than 2.3 million real property accounts across 23 counties, Baltimore City and 155 incorporated municipalities. The state, each county and each municipality set separate rates, and nothing caps them at the state level. When a proposed rate is higher than the current one, the governing body must advertise it and hold a public hearing.

One address can receive two bills, one from the county and one from a town or city. Have the title company verify that both are paid at closing.

Typical tax rates

The State's real property rate is $0.112 per $100 of assessed value, and county rates differ widely on top of it. In the FY 2022-23 rate sheet, Baltimore City was highest at 2.2480 per $100, followed by Baltimore County at 1.1000, Frederick at 1.0600, Garrett at 1.0560 and Howard at 1.0140. Prince George's was 1.0000 and Anne Arundel 0.9330, with Wicomico at 0.9070 and Worcester at 0.8450. Montgomery was lowest of those at 0.6940.

Treat those county figures as a snapshot and ask the county for this year's rate. A bill equals the assessment times the jurisdiction's rate, so a house in Baltimore City and an identical one in Montgomery County can carry very different taxes. Municipal governments set their own rates as well.

How often homes are reassessed

Each property gets a fresh assessment every third year. Counties are divided into three regions, which puts roughly a third of accounts under review annually. Notices go out in late December from SDAT, showing old and new market values along with an appeal form.

Increases are phased in evenly over three years. A value rising from $100,000 to $130,000 is taxed at $110,000, then $120,000, then $130,000. A decrease takes effect right away.

The 2026 cycle covered Group 2 and brought a 12.7% overall increase in assessed value, with residential up an average of 13.2% and commercial up 11%. That compares with 20.1% in the 2025 cycle and 23.4% in 2023. Those are statewide averages, so your own notice is the number that counts.

Due dates and penalties

Payment is due July 1, and no interest accrues through September 30. Past that date the account is in arrears under Tax-Property § 10-102.

  • Bills are mailed in July or August for the fiscal year beginning July 1.
  • Counties and municipalities must offer a semiannual schedule for owner-occupied principal residences. The first installment is due July 1 and payable without interest through September 30, and the second is due December 1 and payable without interest through December 31.
  • The second installment can be prepaid through September 30 with no service charge.
  • After that date, a service charge of up to 1.5% of the second installment applies, plus capped administrative costs.

Interest after the overdue date is set locally. It runs 1% per month in Anne Arundel County and 1.5% per month in Allegany County, so call your own county's collector for the current rule.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin at the local assessment office, within 45 days of the notice date. The appeal can go through four levels, each with its own clock.

LevelDeadlineWho decides
Supervisor's level45 days from the notice dateAn assessor designated by the Supervisor of Assessments
Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board30 days from the final noticeLocal residents appointed by the Governor
Maryland Tax Court30 days from the board's orderAn independent body, in-person hearing
Circuit CourtFurther appealReviews the record for legal error

Neither the board nor the Tax Court charges a filing fee. SDAT tries to finish reassessment appeals by June 1, and the Supervisor's hearing is informal and usually about 15 minutes.

What evidence helps in an appeal?

Market-value evidence carries weight at a hearing. Complaints about the size of the bill carry none. Explain why the Total New Market Value doesn't reflect market value, point out errors on the property worksheet such as a wrong bathroom or fireplace count, and bring comparable sales.

Leave out past values, percentage increases, metropolitan cost arguments, tax bill amounts, and services received or not received. At the Tax Court, any outside properties you plan to cite must be listed at least 10 days in advance with sale date and price or assessment details.

Buyers have a separate path. If a property transfers between January 1 and June 30, the new owner can file a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, once the deed is recorded in the land records. Owners can also file a petition for review by the first working day after January 1 in the two years when the property isn't being reassessed, if they believe value has fallen.

Tax credits and deferrals

The main programs are the Homestead Tax Credit, the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit and a deferral for older owners.

  • Homestead Tax Credit: applies when a principal residence's taxable assessment rises more than the local cap, which is 10% or lower. One application establishes eligibility.
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit: an income-based sliding scale that has delivered over $58 million in credits, with a $60,000 household income ceiling.
  • Property tax deferral: open to owners 65 or older where the local government has adopted it. The deferred amount becomes a lien and is repaid on transfer.

Religious, charitable and educational organizations may be exempt on property they own and use, and so may government property.

What happens if property tax goes unpaid?

A county may auction the tax lien, yet the homeowner remains the owner. The buyer receives a tax lien certificate and may later ask a court to foreclose the right of redemption.

At least 30 days before the first advertisement, the Collector mails the owner of record a notice of the taxes owed. The sale is then advertised weekly for four successive weeks. A buyer can file a foreclosure case no earlier than six months after the sale, or nine months for owner-occupied homes under state law and in Baltimore City, and must file within two years of the certificate date or it becomes void.

Redemption stays open until the court forecloses, and it takes payment of the sale price, interest, later taxes and penalties in certified funds. If redemption happens more than four months after the sale, the owner also reimburses the certificate holder's expenses and attorney's fees. The State Tax Sale Ombudsman can be reached at (833) 732-8411.

Selling with taxes owed

Overdue property tax becomes a lien, and a tax sale grows out of it. In some counties water, sewer or special charges ride along.

If you're behind, get the exact payoff and sale date from the county. The payoff letter goes to the title company, which pays the lien out of your proceeds. If a tax sale has already happened, ask the Ombudsman or the county for the redemption figure and the deadline. Costs rise the longer the lien sits, so the earlier you call, the smaller the number. A cash buyer can close on a short timeline, which helps when the clock on redemption is running.

Frequently asked questions

When are Maryland property taxes due?

They are due July 1 and can be paid without interest through September 30. Owner-occupied homes can use a semiannual plan, with the second installment due December 1.

How long do I have to appeal my Maryland assessment?

You have 45 days from the date on the assessment notice. The next appeal goes to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice.

How often does Maryland reassess property?

Every three years. Increases are phased in evenly over three years, and decreases take effect immediately.

Do I lose my house if I miss a property tax payment?

Not right away. The county sells the tax lien, and the owner keeps the property and can redeem it until a court forecloses the right of redemption.

Can a buyer appeal an assessment after purchase?

Yes, for a transfer between January 1 and June 30. The buyer files a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, after the deed is recorded.

What the Maryland homestead credit does

In Maryland, "homestead" usually means the Homestead Property Tax Credit. It limits how fast the taxable assessment on your principal residence can climb. It does not knock a fixed dollar amount off the value of your home.

Every county and municipality must hold annual increases in taxable assessment to 10% or less. The credit appears on a bill only in years when the phased-in assessment grows faster than the cap. In a flat year you may see no credit at all, and that does not mean your application was lost.

For a seller the credit matters in two ways. It has been lowering the bill you carry now, and it does not travel with the house. A buyer has to qualify on their own after the deed is recorded.

How the credit is calculated

The credit is the portion of the assessment increase above the cap, multiplied by the tax rate. Under Tax-Property § 9-105(e), State and bicounty taxes use a fixed 110% of the prior year's taxable assessment, while each county or municipality picks a percentage between 100% and 110% for its own tax.

Think of it in steps. Start with last year's taxable assessment, then find the new phased-in assessment. Apply the cap to get the highest assessment the bill may use. Whatever sits above that limit is shielded, and the credit equals the tax on that shielded amount at the applicable rate.

Credits under $1 are not granted. Each county sets its own local cap, so check the county's current tax rate sheet for the percentage that applies to your address.

Who qualifies?

You qualify if the house is your principal residence, you hold a legal interest in it, and nothing in the prior year disqualified the property. The conditions:

  • You live in the home at least six months of the year, including July 1 of the credit year. Illness or a need for special care can excuse an absence.
  • You claim the credit on one property only.
  • The property was not transferred to new ownership in the prior tax year.
  • The owner did not request a zoning change that raised the value, and the use of the property did not change substantially.
  • The prior assessment was not clearly erroneous.

Section 9-105 defines a homeowner broadly. Sole ownership, joint ownership, tenancy by the entireties, a cooperative membership, a land installment contract and a life estate can all count as a legal interest.

There are carve-outs. If an accident or natural disaster damages the home, eligibility can continue for the current year and two more. An owner who razes the house or makes substantial improvements keeps eligibility by having lived there as a principal residence for at least three full tax years before the work, and by finishing within the next tax year. Federal employees stationed outside Maryland can keep it for up to six consecutive years.

How to apply and check your status

You file one application, and it carries forward as long as you keep qualifying. A 2007 law (Tax-Property § 9-105) created the one-time requirement, and the Maryland One Stop portal has taken applications since September 11, 2023.

  • Apply online at Maryland One Stop or through the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) homestead site.
  • Download the paper form in English or Spanish and mail it to the Homestead Tax Credit Division, 700 East Pratt Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 2700, Baltimore, MD 21202, or fax it to 410-225-9344.
  • Do not email an application that contains a Social Security number or a tax return.
  • Look up your property in SDAT's Real Property search. A status of Approved or Application Received needs no action, while No Application means you should file.

The SDAT questions line is 410-767-2165 in the Baltimore area and 1-866-650-8783 elsewhere in Maryland. A final denial can be appealed within 30 days to the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board for the property's jurisdiction. The statute refers to May 1 as a date for the application, so file as early as you can.

When you sell a Maryland house

The credit ends for you at the sale, since a transfer for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year. The new owner must file their own application.

The state works to make that hand-off hard to miss. Since 2021 (Chapter 333), a residential sales contract must carry a statement that a buyer who plans to live in the home may qualify for the homestead property tax credit, plus the SDAT web address. Under § 9-105(f), the settlement agent must give the buyer the application document at settlement, and SDAT mails an application to new owners once the deed is recorded and its records update.

One timing rule helps in a few sales. If a deed is dated in one year but recorded between July 1 and September 1 of the next, the buyer can ask SDAT to treat the deed date as the transfer date. The request is due by September 1 of the second year after the deed date and must include a copy of the executed deed.

Inherited houses follow different rules, covered next.

Heirs and the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit

Heirs not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while the title transfer is finalized. They need the will, trust or other instrument, a death certificate, proof of relationship, and the names and addresses of all heirs.

This is a separate program with its own tests. Combined gross household income cannot exceed $60,000, and net worth, not counting the home or qualified retirement savings, must be under $200,000. Only tax on the first $300,000 of assessed value counts, and water and sewer charges are not covered.

Household incomeTax limit
$8,000$0
$12,000$160
$16,000$420
$20,000$780
$25,000$1,230
$30,000$1,680

The credit is the amount by which your property tax exceeds that limit. Call SDAT to confirm the current figures. Apply by April 15 to see the credit on the July bill. The filing deadline is October 1 each year. Buyers should apply at least 30 days before settlement to receive the credit at the closing table.

Homestead protection from creditors

The exemptions in Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 11-504 are small, and the one for an owner-occupied home applies only in bankruptcy. A debtor can elect up to $6,000 in cash or property within 30 days of attachment or levy, and up to $500 in a bank account is exempt without electing, with the two combined capped at $6,000.

In a bankruptcy case, § 11-504 also covers owner-occupied residential property, including a condominium or cooperative unit used as a home, up to the federal amount in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) adjusted for inflation. Spouses cannot both claim it in the same case, and an eight-year lookback applies to earlier successful claims on the same property.

This is a different idea from the tax credit, and the two are easy to confuse. A seller facing judgments, liens or a pending bankruptcy should talk with a Maryland attorney before signing a contract.

Penalties for claiming the credit wrongly

Someone who does not qualify must pay all the property tax otherwise due for each year of ineligibility. Willful misrepresentation adds a penalty of 25% of the credit received for each affected year, and that penalty becomes a lien on the property.

That lien is why a seller should confirm the status of a former second home or a rented-out house before listing. Owners should report a property that has stopped being a principal residence to the local assessment office by email or phone. A lien of that kind is a title issue and must be cleared before closing.

Selling for cash with the credit in play

A cash sale leaves the tax rules alone but shortens the time you have to tidy things up. Before accepting an offer, gather your latest tax bill, the SDAT property record showing your homestead status, and any notice about a prior-year credit.

  • Ask SDAT or your local assessment office whether the status shows Approved.
  • Check whether any tax is unpaid or any credit has been reversed.
  • If you are an heir, confirm whether you are on the record title yet.

Because the credit does not transfer, your buyer's first bill after closing can look different from yours. That is normal and reflects the buyer's own application, not an error in the sale.

Frequently asked questions

Does Maryland have a homestead exemption?

Maryland has a Homestead Property Tax Credit and no flat exemption. It limits yearly increases in the taxable assessment on your principal residence to 10% or less, and local governments may set a lower cap.

Do I have to reapply every year?

No. The homestead application is a one-time filing. The separate Homeowners' Tax Credit is applied for each year, with an October 1 deadline.

Does the credit transfer to the buyer when I sell?

No. A sale for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year, so the buyer must file a new application. The settlement agent is required to hand the buyer the application at closing.

How do I know if I already have the credit?

Search the property in SDAT's Real Property database. Approved or Application Received means no action is needed, and No Application means you should file.

Can I keep the credit on a house I inherited?

Possibly for a limited time. Heirs not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while title is finalized, with documents such as the will and death certificate.

Estate tax versus inheritance tax

Maryland has two separate death taxes. The estate tax is charged on the estate as a whole. The inheritance tax is charged on what each person receives. A house can trigger one, both or neither, depending on the size of the estate and who ends up owning the property.

The estate tax applies to the estates of Maryland residents and to nonresidents who own Maryland real property or tangible personal property located in the state. Its rates follow a federal credit schedule as it stood on December 31, 2001, topping out at 16 percent above $10,040,000 of adjusted taxable estate. Inheritance tax paid in Maryland can be credited against the estate tax.

The inheritance tax works from the other direction. Under Tax-General § 7-202 it is a tax on the privilege of receiving property from someone who has died, when that property has a taxable situs in Maryland. The recipient is the one it reaches.

Tax law in this area changes, so ask the Comptroller which rules cover your family's date of death before relying on any figure here.

Estate tax exclusion by year of death

For a death in 2019 or later, the exclusion is $5,000,000 plus any unused exclusion carried over from a deceased spouse. Tax-General § 7-309 phased it in: $1,000,000 for deaths before 2015, $1,500,000 in 2015, $2,000,000 in 2016, $3,000,000 in 2017 and $4,000,000 in 2018.

The same section bars a deduction for state death taxes under federal code section 2058, and it caps the federal credit used in the Maryland calculation at 16 percent of the taxable estate above the exclusion. When a federal return is required, or would be required under the lower Maryland exclusion, § 7-305 makes the Maryland return due nine months after death. A return filed only to elect the spouse's unused exclusion follows the federal deadline for that election. An amended return is due within 90 days after the filer learns the tax has gone up.

Family farms

Yes, Maryland gives a break to estates with a family farm. Up to $5,000,000 of qualified agricultural property can be left out of the gross estate if it passes to a qualified recipient who agrees to keep farming. On the Eastern Shore and in Western Maryland, a farmhouse and its land are often one parcel, so this comes up often.

When farm property is worth more than $5,000,000, § 7-309(c) adds a second layer: 16 percent on the taxable estate above the exclusion (leaving the farm out of that figure), plus 5 percent of the farm value above $5,000,000. If the land stops being farmed within 10 years of the death, extra tax is recaptured. The inheritance tax has its own farmland rule. Real property under a perpetual farming easement that passes to a niece or nephew is exempt, with recapture if farming ends.

Heirs who inherit a farmhouse and want to sell to someone who will not farm should ask the estate's attorney whether either recapture rule applies before signing a contract.

Who pays the 10 percent inheritance tax?

People outside the close family circle pay it. Tax-General § 7-204 sets the rate at 10 percent of the clear value of property passing from the decedent, and clear value is fair market value minus expenses.

Section 7-203(b) exempts property passing to a long list of relatives. The Register of Wills fills in who is taxed and who is not:

RecipientTreatment
Spouse, parent, grandparent, child, stepchild, sibling, lineal descendantsExempt (§ 7-203(b))
Niece, nephew, aunt, uncle, cousinTaxed at 10 percent (nieces and nephews are exempt only for easement farmland)
Friend or unrelated individualTaxed at 10 percent, subject to listed exceptions
Registered domestic partner (death on or after October 1, 2023)Exempt
Other domestic partner (death on or after July 1, 2009)Taxed, except a primary residence held jointly with survivorship, with an affidavit or two proofs of partnership
Qualifying 501(c)(3) charity; State, county or municipalityExempt

A corporation, partnership or LLC owned entirely by exempt relatives is also exempt. Most wills carry a tax clause that makes the estate pay for a will beneficiary. Without one, the legatee pays, and an heir in an intestate estate pays personally.

Property outside the inheritance tax

Some property is outside the tax no matter who receives it. Section 7-203 exempts the following:

  • Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the estate
  • Up to $500 left in a will for grave upkeep
  • Property passing to any one person if it totals $1,000 or less
  • Property distributed through a small estate under Estates and Trusts § 5-601
  • Income and gains on probate assets earned after the date of death
  • Qualifying public and private employee benefit plan payments
  • Personal property of nonresident decedents when reciprocity applies, though not tangible property located in Maryland

The small estate exemption is the one that reaches most homes with little equity. A small estate means probate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less when the spouse is the sole heir or legatee, valued at fair market value less debts secured by the property.

How the Register of Wills collects

The Register of Wills in the relevant county sets and collects the inheritance tax. When an estate is administered in court, the personal representative files an Administration Account showing who received what, and the payment goes in with that account.

Property that passes outside probate is handled by invoice. The Register bills from the Information Report or an Application to Fix Inheritance Tax. Under § 7-214, when there is no formal administration, the Register in the county where the inventory is filed makes the determination and bills each person responsible. Late invoices escalate on a schedule:

  • After 30 days without payment, a 10 percent penalty and interest are added and a second invoice goes out.
  • At 60 days from the first invoice, more interest applies and a third invoice is sent.
  • At 90 days, the full amount goes to the Maryland Central Collection Unit, which may add interest at up to 18 percent.

Heirs who plan to sell should ask the Register what has been billed before counting on the proceeds.

Selling an inherited Maryland house

Nobody can sell estate property until the Register of Wills or the Orphans' Court has appointed a personal representative. That appointment must come before any asset is disposed of, and if real property is sold, a copy of the closing disclosure goes in with the First Account.

The usual sequence:

  • File the original will with the Register of Wills in the county where the decedent lived.
  • Get a personal representative appointed.
  • File a List of Interested Persons within 20 days of appointment in a regular estate.
  • File the inventory within three months, listing the house at fair market value as of the date of death.
  • File the account, which is where inheritance tax is determined and paid.

The personal representative's commission is capped at 9 percent when the property is $20,000 or less, and at $1,800 plus 3.6 percent of the excess above that. Probate fees are charged when the First Account is filed, and they rise with the size of the estate.

If the house needs repairs or the heirs live far away, a cash sale can shorten the time the estate carries utilities, insurance and taxes. The sale still waits for the appointment, so start that step first.

Frequently asked questions

Does Maryland have an inheritance tax?

Yes. Maryland charges 10 percent on the clear value of property passing to people who are not close relatives. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings and lineal descendants are exempt under Tax-General § 7-203(b).

Do children pay inheritance tax on an inherited house?

No. Property passing to a child, stepchild or other lineal descendant is exempt. A niece, nephew, cousin or friend who inherits the same house owes 10 percent of its clear value.

When is the Maryland estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death, when a federal return is required or would be required under the lower Maryland exclusion. A return filed only to claim a spouse's unused exclusion follows the federal deadline for that election.

Can heirs sell an inherited house before the estate closes?

Yes, once a personal representative has been appointed. That appointment is required before any asset is disposed of, and a copy of the closing disclosure is filed with the First Account.

What if the inheritance tax invoice goes unpaid?

The Register adds a 10 percent penalty and interest after 30 days and sends more invoices. At 90 days the debt goes to the Central Collection Unit, which may charge interest at up to 18 percent.

Steps of a Maryland eviction, in order

An eviction runs through the District Court in the county where the property sits, and it cannot end with a sheriff at the door unless the landlord first wins a judgment and obtains a warrant. A rent case follows one basic sequence:

  1. The landlord sends the written notice of intent and waits out the 10-day cure period.
  2. The landlord files a sworn complaint and the court issues a summons.
  3. A rent court hearing takes place, usually on a short schedule.
  4. If the landlord wins, the tenant has a short window to leave or pay.
  5. The landlord petitions for a warrant of restitution, with no hearing.
  6. The landlord gives the final written notice of the eviction date.
  7. A sheriff or constable carries out the eviction.

The notice rules are covered in our Maryland eviction notice guide. This page follows the case once it reaches court.

Cases the District Court hears

Landlords bring five kinds of cases, each with its own paperwork.

Case typeWhat it seeksForm or step
Failure to pay rentEviction and possibly back rentDC-CV-115 notice, then DC-CV-082 complaint
Tenant holding overEviction after the lease endsCourt complaint
Breach of leaseEviction for lease violationsCourt complaint
Wrongful detainerRemoval of someone who is not a lawful occupantCourt complaint
Petition for warrant of restitutionCarrying out a judgment already wonDC-CV-081, no hearing

Tenants have filings of their own, including rent escrow and breach of the warranty of habitability (DC-CV-083) and security deposit claims. Foreclosure cases belong to the circuit courts, not the District Court.

What happens at rent court?

In an unpaid rent case, trial is set for the fifth day after the complaint is filed. Under Real Property § 8-401, the court may adjourn for one day to bring in witnesses, or longer if everyone agrees.

The landlord generally speaks first and the tenant answers. The judge can rule on the spot or set another hearing. If someone fails to appear, the court may dismiss, enter judgment or postpone. A tenant can request a postponement by writing to the clerk before trial and mailing a copy to the landlord.

Service matters. An eviction-only case can go forward on mail plus posting on the property. A money judgment for back rent requires personal service on a residential tenant. Posting can support a default judgment for possession and cannot support one for money owed.

If rent is truly due, the court fixes the amount owed as of the filing date and orders possession surrendered within 4 days after trial. A physician's certificate can stretch that to no more than 15 days. If the tenant pays the rent, late fees and costs at trial or at an adjourned date, the complaint is marked satisfied and there is no eviction.

Paying to stay after a judgment

In most rent cases a tenant can stop the eviction by paying what the judgment says before it is carried out. This is the right of redemption under § 8-401(h). The tenant pays all past-due rent plus the costs and fees the court awarded.

  • A landlord must accept checks from a government agency or government-funded organization.
  • Cash, certified check and money order are accepted forms of payment.
  • A landlord can ask the court to deny redemption when the tenant has had three possession judgments for unpaid rent in the previous 12 months (four in Baltimore City).

A tenant who wants the judgment reviewed can appeal to the circuit court within 4 days in a nonpayment case, and has to post a bond to stay in the home. In breach-of-lease and holdover cases the window is 10 days.

Warrant timing and expiration

In a failure-to-pay-rent case, a landlord should wait 7 business days after the possession judgment before asking for a warrant. Breach-of-lease and holdover judgments allow the request right away. The statute's text in § 8-401(f) says 7 days, so confirm the current waiting period with the District Court clerk before you file.

A warrant has an expiry date too. In a nonpayment case the landlord must order it within 60 days of the later of the judgment or the end of any stay, or the possession judgment is stricken. The same happens if a warrant is ordered and nothing is done within 60 days. A stricken judgment can still count toward the number of judgments that eliminates redemption rights.

With the warrant in hand, the landlord must send the final notice at least 6 days ahead. If the sheriff has doubts about that notice, or the tenant may have redeemed, the sheriff must tell the District Court and wait for a further order.

Eviction day

A sheriff or constable has to be present. The ground rules:

  • No evictions on Sundays or holidays.
  • The landlord does not have to give the exact day in advance, beyond the 6-day window notice.
  • Once belongings are removed, the tenant is responsible for them.
  • The sheriff checks for dogs or cats. If the tenant is present the animal is handed over, and if not, the sheriff provides shelter or rescue contact information.
  • Baltimore City has extra notice and property-removal rules.

Weather can postpone the day. For residential property, the warrant is stayed day to day during extreme weather, including temperatures of 32 degrees Fahrenheit or lower and certain National Weather Service winter, hurricane, tropical storm or excessive heat warnings. After conditions end, the eviction must be finished within 5 days. Government employees furloughed during a shutdown may also qualify for a stay, generally no longer than 30 days past the shutdown's end.

If the tenant is not home, the officer posts a notice on the front door saying repossession is complete. A tenant who proves the landlord broke the notice rules can recover actual damages, attorney's fees and injunctive relief.

Tenant help, and what owners selling should know

Tenants with household income at or below 50 percent of the state median may qualify for a free lawyer through the Access to Counsel in Evictions program, reached by calling 211. The Maryland Court Help Center takes calls at 410-260-1392, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.

An owner thinking of selling a rented house should know the sale carries tenant protections of its own. Before listing a house with three or fewer units, the owner generally must give a tenant of at least six months a written chance to make an offer under § 8-119. Exceptions cover foreclosure transfers, estate fiduciaries, inheritance and family sales.

A landlord also cannot force the issue. Section 8-216 bars lockouts and utility shutoffs, and the only lawful ways to regain possession are a court warrant carried out by a sheriff or constable, or an abandonment or surrender by the tenant.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Maryland eviction take?

The statutes set short steps and no single total. Trial is the fifth day after filing, possession is due within 4 days after trial, then the warrant request follows and the landlord gives at least 6 days written notice. Postponements, appeals and weather stays add time.

Can a tenant pay and stay after a judgment?

Usually yes, by paying all past-due rent plus court-awarded costs and fees before the eviction is carried out. A landlord can ask the court to deny redemption after three possession judgments in 12 months (four in Baltimore City).

Which court handles evictions in Maryland?

The District Court in the county where the property is located. Circuit courts handle foreclosure cases and appeals from District Court landlord-tenant judgments.

Does the sheriff have to be there for an eviction?

Yes. A sheriff or constable carries out the warrant of restitution, and evictions are not allowed on Sundays or holidays.

Can a landlord sell a rented house during an eviction case?

Yes, but tenant protections still apply. For a rental of three or fewer units, a tenant of six months or more generally gets a written chance to make an offer before the owner lists the property.

What a transfer on death deed is

It is a deed that names who gets a house when the owner dies, signed and recorded while the owner is alive. Maryland's version took effect October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738, Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws.

The new subtitle sits in Real Property Article 14-1001 and following. The owner stays in control for life: the deed gives the named beneficiary no ownership until death. It works much like a beneficiary designation on a bank account or life insurance policy.

The Act applies to a deed made before, on or after October 1, 2026, if the owner dies on or after that date. Talk with an estate planning attorney about drafting and recording, and about how the deed fits with a will and the rest of the plan.

  • Owner: called the transferor in the statute.
  • Beneficiary: the person or people named to receive the property.
  • Joint owners: owners with survivorship rights, such as tenants by the entirety, are treated differently from tenants in common.

Who can sign one and what it must say

Any owner with the capacity needed to make a will can sign one. The deed must follow the execution rules in Estates and Trusts 4-101 and must state that the transfer to the beneficiary happens at the owner's death.

The statutory form in 14-1011 includes owner and beneficiary information, a legal description, the transfer-at-death statement, and preparer and notary sections. Witnesses and notaries can't be relatives of the owners or beneficiaries, or beneficiaries themselves.

A deed can name one beneficiary or several. If it names several without saying how they hold title, they take as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. A deed can also name alternate beneficiaries, including successive alternates, who take if a primary beneficiary doesn't survive the owner.

Recording and taxes

The deed must be recorded in the land records of the county where the house sits before the owner dies, or it has no effect. Signing it is not enough.

Recording follows Real Property 3-104 with several changes the Act makes for TOD deeds. The collector's endorsement, certain intake sheet and assessment office endorsements, and the attorney or party preparation certification don't apply. The clerk may still refuse a TOD deed that comes without an intake sheet. The assessment records don't change to the beneficiary's name until the owner's death.

TopicRule under Chapter 751
When it takes effectAt the owner's death, if recorded before then
Notice to beneficiaryNot required during the owner's life
ConsiderationNot required
State recordation tax and state and county transfer taxExempt if primary or secondary residence of the owner
Inheritance taxBeneficiaries may still owe it

The exemptions rest on Tax-Property 12-108, 13-207 and 13-414.

What the owner can still do while alive

Almost everything. The deed doesn't change the owner's right to live in, sell or mortgage the house, and it doesn't give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.

Section 14-1007 spells out what a recorded TOD deed doesn't do during the owner's life.

  • It doesn't limit the owner's right to sell or encumber the property.
  • It doesn't affect a buyer's or lender's rights, even if they know about the deed.
  • It doesn't affect the rights of the owner's creditors, including future ones.
  • It doesn't affect eligibility for public assistance, including Medicaid, for the owner or the beneficiary.
  • It doesn't expose the house to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

That is a real difference from adding a relative to the title as a joint owner, which can expose the house to that person's creditors, lawsuits or divorce and gives them present rights.

Changing or revoking the deed

You change or revoke it by recording a new document before the owner dies. A TOD deed is always revocable, even if the deed itself says otherwise.

There are three ways to revoke all or part of a recorded deed, each recorded in the county land records.

  • A new TOD deed that expressly revokes the earlier one or conflicts with it.
  • An instrument of revocation that says so expressly.
  • A lifetime deed that expressly revokes the TOD deed.

A will can't revoke a recorded TOD deed, and neither can marking up the deed itself. With joint owners, a deed is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke. A TOD deed naming a spouse is revoked automatically by divorce or annulment, and it is also revoked if the owner later marries and has a child by birth, adoption or legitimation.

What happens when the owner dies

Title passes to the surviving beneficiary by operation of law, without probate for that house. The beneficiary takes subject to any existing mortgage, lien, security interest or encumbrance, and the transfer carries no warranty of title.

If a beneficiary doesn't survive the owner, that share lapses, and an alternate takes if one is named. A beneficiary who intentionally killed the owner is disqualified, and the Act keeps the rights of pretermitted children and the elective share of a spouse in play. Any beneficiary may disclaim, and for real property the disclaimer must be recorded in the county land records.

Section 14-1013 creates an optional Notification of Death form. The statute sets no deadline to record it, and the transfer happens at death whether or not it is recorded. Recording it still matters, because the clerk forwards it to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation so the property records can be updated. If a beneficiary who lives in the house uses the form's occupancy option, the beneficiary certifies under penalty of perjury to live there as a principal residence for at least 7 of the next 12 months.

Selling a house held under a TOD deed

The owner can sell the house any time while alive without the beneficiary's consent. After death, the beneficiary can sell once title has moved to them and the paperwork is in order.

A beneficiary who inherits through a TOD deed takes a house with whatever debt is attached. A buyer or title company may ask to see the recorded TOD deed and the notification of death, if one was recorded. Gather the recorded deed, a certified death certificate and any mortgage statement before you list, so the closing doesn't stall on paperwork.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including inherited homes. If you are a beneficiary and the house needs repairs or has back taxes, call us before you spend money on repairs. If you are an owner thinking about a TOD deed and a sale, remember that the deed doesn't stop you from selling while you are alive.

Before relying on a TOD deed, check the tax effects, existing liens, multiple beneficiaries, possible family disputes and Medicaid or long-term care planning.

Frequently asked questions

When did Maryland's transfer on death deed take effect?

October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738 (Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws). It covers deeds made before, on or after that date if the owner dies on or after it.

Does a TOD deed have to be recorded?

Yes. It is effective only if recorded in the land records of the county where the property is located before the owner's death.

Can I still sell my house if I record a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed doesn't limit your right to sell or mortgage the property, and it doesn't give the beneficiary any interest while you are alive.

Does a will override a TOD deed in Maryland?

No. A recorded TOD deed can't be revoked by a will. It can be revoked by a recorded new TOD deed, a recorded revocation, or a recorded lifetime deed.

Does a TOD deed avoid inheritance tax?

No. The recordation and transfer taxes are exempt for a residence, but beneficiaries may still owe inheritance tax.

Taxes on a Maryland seller's closing statement

Expect three government charges on a Maryland settlement sheet. One is the statewide transfer tax at 0.5% of the sale consideration. The other two, a county transfer tax and a recordation tax, depend on the county.

They attach to the deed, so an agent's involvement changes nothing. The circuit court clerk also adds a recording fee and a surcharge, and the tax account must be current before the deed can go through.

  • State transfer tax: 0.5% of consideration, collected at the clerk's counter.
  • County transfer tax: each county picks a rate between 0% and 1.5%.
  • Recordation tax: a county rate applied to every $500 of consideration.
  • Recording fee and surcharge: assessed on each instrument filed.
  • Back taxes and county charges: settled first.

Who pays transfer and recordation taxes?

The default under Real Property Article 14-104 is a 50-50 split of the recordation tax and both transfer taxes. A contract or another statute can change that, and most Maryland contracts speak to it, so find that clause before signing.

A major exception applies to first-time Maryland buyers who intend to occupy the home as their principal residence. In that case the seller covers the entire State transfer tax, and the recordation and local transfer taxes as well, unless both sides agree in writing to a different arrangement.

There are conditions. Every buyer named on the deed signs a sworn statement, and with several buyers all of them must qualify. The State rate for these buyers drops to 0.25% from 0.5%, which lowers the seller's cost on that one line.

A local government may also exempt part of the recordation tax for owner-occupied homes where the buyer lives for at least 7 months of a 12 month period. Your title company or clerk will know whether your county has done so.

County rates compared

Rates swing widely from county to county, and an identical price can mean very different bills. Here are fiscal 2026 rates for five counties.

CountyRecordation tax (per $500)County transfer tax
Baltimore County$2.501.5%
Howard$2.501.25%
Harford$3.301.0%
Carroll$6.500.0%
Frederick$7.000.0%

Montgomery County's rate varies with property value and adds a recordation surcharge on transactions over $500,000. Anne Arundel's transfer tax runs from 1.0% to 1.5%. Across the state, recordation tax ranges from $2.50 to $7.00 per $500, and transfer tax from 0% to 1.5%.

Under the default split each side carries half. With a qualifying first-time buyer the State rate falls to 0.25% and the seller carries the whole set unless the contract says otherwise. A title company can put an estimate for your own address in writing.

Recording fees and surcharges

Recording a typical deed of nine pages or less costs $20 at the circuit court clerk's office, and nearly every recorded instrument also carries a $40 surcharge. Harford and Howard Counties show identical figures.

  • Release of nine pages or less: $10.
  • Instrument of ten pages or more that is not a principal residence: $75.
  • Copies: $0.50 a page in Harford County, plus $5 for a certified copy.
  • Harford Land Records accepts e-records through Simplifile.

Recording fees are not refundable, and getting State transfer tax back takes a claim form filed with the clerk. If an exemption applies, the document must quote the complete exemption code, or the clerk collects full tax.

Property tax before the deed transfers

Under Real Property Article 3-104, all taxes, assessments and charges owed on the property must be paid first. The collector then endorses a certificate on the deed, and only after that is the transfer posted to the assessment books. Some counties charge up to $55 for the certificate of paid charges.

Procedures are local. Harford County sells a Certificate of Tax Liens and Other Charges Due for $50, valid 90 days, and county staff stamp each deed before recording. In Howard County, deeds pass through the Department of Finance's Division of Recordation Tax before they reach Land Records.

Back taxes catch sellers off guard more than anything else. Liens are auctioned at annual tax sales. Even then, the owner can redeem by paying the lien amount, interest and fees up to the moment a circuit judge signs a foreclosure order.

Where the county steps happen

Closing paperwork goes through a tax office that collects and stamps, then the Circuit Court land records office that records. Harford and Howard show how much hours and timing can differ.

  • Harford Revenue Collections: 220 S. Main Street, Bel Air, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, with processing that usually takes 24 to 48 hours.
  • Harford Land Records: 20 West Courtland Street, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a 4:00 p.m. courier and title company cutoff.
  • Howard Division of Recordation Tax: 3430 Courthouse Drive, Ellicott City, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Howard Land Records: 9250 Judicial Way, Suite 1900, with recording hours of 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

Harford allows walk-ins no more than five documents or sets at a time. The tax office stamps the deed before the clerk records it, so leave a couple of days between the two.

Sellers who live out of state

If you live outside Maryland, 8.75% of the total payment is held back at settlement when you are an individual, and 8.25% when you are an entity. Form MW506NRS reports the withholding, and recording waits for the payment.

Think of it as an advance on your income tax rather than a true closing cost. An early refund request is available if you owe less and the price is under $1.5 million. Our Maryland capital gains guide has the full rules.

Closing costs in a direct cash sale

Paying cash does not shrink these charges, since they attach to the deed and the tax account. What a cash contract decides is who covers each line.

Ask for a written net sheet with every tax line itemized before you sign. Then confirm three things with your attorney or title company: first-time buyer status, which party pays the county transfer and recordation taxes, and the balance the county shows on the tax account.

On closing day the order of events is predictable. The title company or attorney collects the tax certificate, the deed goes to the county tax office for a stamp, and then it moves to the clerk for recording. The taxes and fees come out of your proceeds unless the contract assigns them to the buyer, so the net sheet is the only way to know what you will actually receive. Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the final settlement statement for your own tax records.

Frequently asked questions

Who covers the transfer tax?

Absent a contrary contract term, each party pays half of the State and local transfer taxes and the recordation tax. With a first-time buyer moving in, the seller covers the full State tax and, by default, the local taxes.

What is the State transfer tax rate?

Half a percent (0.5%) of consideration. A first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the home pays the lower 0.25% rate, all of it paid by the seller.

How much is the recordation tax in Maryland?

It depends on the county, per $500 of consideration: $2.50 in Howard and Baltimore Counties, $3.30 in Harford and $7.00 in Frederick.

Do Maryland sellers pay a recording fee?

Yes, a $20 fee for most short deeds plus a $40 surcharge. The contract says who bears it.

Does property tax have to be paid before closing?

Yes. Everything owed must be paid and the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed before the county posts the transfer.

Which office handles probate

Each of Maryland's 24 jurisdictions has its own Register of Wills and its own Orphans' Court. The 24 are the state's 23 counties and Baltimore City, and you file in the jurisdiction where the person who died lived.

The Register is an elected official, chosen every four years, who handles the paperwork of administrative probate. The Orphans' Court steps in for disputes and for judicial probate. In Harford, Howard and Montgomery Counties a Circuit Court judge serves as the Orphans' Court, and the other 21 jurisdictions elect three judges to four-year terms.

A family selling an inherited house starts by finding the right office. The state's Registers of Wills website lists them by county.

Types of estates

Maryland sorts estates into small, regular, modified and judicial. The label depends on asset value, who inherits and whether anyone contests the will.

TypeWho it fitsNotable features
Small estateProbate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less if the spouse is the only heir or legateeNo fee to file the petition, and no inheritance tax collected on probate property
Regular estateProbate assets above those amountsInventory, accounts and a fuller notice process
Modified administrationA solvent regular estate for a death on or after October 1, 1997, where residual takers are the personal representative and certain tax-exempt people or entitiesFinal report instead of an inventory and accounts
Judicial probateCases where the will is questioned or damaged, or more than one qualified person appliesRun by the Orphans' Court

Assets in the decedent's sole name or held as tenants in common count as probate assets. For anything that passes another way, ask the Register or an attorney.

Steps and deadlines in a regular estate

A regular estate follows a fixed calendar. It starts with the petition and runs about nine months to the first account. The milestones:

  • File the original will with the Register, then the Petition for Administration (Form 1112) and Schedule A (Form 1136), promptly after death.
  • File the List of Interested Persons with the petition or within 20 days of appointment.
  • Publish the Notice of Appointment for three consecutive weeks and supply copies for mailing within 20 days.
  • File the inventory and information report within three months of appointment.
  • File the first account within nine months.

Small estates move faster. The information report is due within three months of appointment, and where no formal administration is opened an Application to Fix Tax on Non-Probate Assets is due within 90 days of death. Modified administration compresses the ending, with a final report due within 10 months and distribution within 12.

Can the personal representative sell the house without court approval?

Usually yes. Under Estates and Trusts § 7-401, a personal representative can act without court approval and may sell, mortgage, exchange or lease estate property, unless the will limits those powers.

Timing is the catch. Duties and powers begin when the Register issues Letters of Administration. A family member who hasn't been appointed can't sign a deed for the estate, so the Letters come before any deed.

The same section lets a personal representative keep assets until sale, pay valid claims, insure property, pay funeral, tax and administration costs, and borrow money. The role is a fiduciary one, held to the highest standard of care, and a representative who falls short can be personally liable.

Valuing an inherited house for the inventory

For a regular estate, real property can be valued at its full cash value for property tax assessment, or at the arm's-length contract sales price if settlement happens within one year of death. The second option helps when you sell quickly.

Small estates use fair market value less debts of record secured by the property at death. Appraisals containing words such as approximate aren't accepted for the inventory, and values are as of the date of death. Assessment values can't be used for farmland, woodland or land on a national registry.

Maryland also lets residential property from an estate pass to an heir with taxes due at recording paid under a payment plan, under Real Property § 3-104. If the heir sells soon after, clear up the plan and the title steps with the settlement company.

Who can serve as personal representative

Most adults can serve, with a few exclusions, and a bond is often part of the process. Disqualified people include anyone under 18, a person found mentally incompetent, those with certain serious convictions unless good cause is shown, and non-citizens unless they are permanent residents who are a spouse, ancestor, descendant or sibling of the decedent.

  • A nonresident must file an irrevocable designation of a Maryland resident agent (Form 1106).
  • In a small estate, a bond (Form 1115) is required when the estate is $10,000 or more after allowable expenses, unless the will excuses it or all interested persons waive it.
  • In a regular estate, a nominal bond is used when bond is excused or waived, and an insurance company must execute any bond.

Anyone holding the original will must deposit it with the Register promptly after death. A custodian who willfully refuses to deliver a will after notice of death can be liable for resulting damages.

Creditors get paid before heirs

Creditors are paid first, in a set order, and the house may have to be sold to cover them. A claim must be presented by the earlier of six months after death or 30 days after the creditor receives written notice that the claim will be barred. The Department of Health has its own period, running to the earlier of six months after the appointment notice is published or two months after it receives notice.

If the estate can't pay everyone, the order is:

  • Register fees, then administration costs and expenses
  • Funeral expenses up to $15,000
  • Personal representative compensation, legal services and real estate broker commissions
  • Family allowance, child support and the decedent's taxes
  • Last-illness bills, up to three months of rent arrears, and wages from the final three months

Debts owed to the federal government, such as IRS taxes, have absolute priority under federal law.

Probate costs and inheritance tax

Fees rise with the value of the estate, and the inheritance tax depends on who receives the property. The probate fee is $0 for an estate under $50,000, $100 from $50,000 to under $100,000, $200 from $100,000 to under $500,000, and $1,000 from $500,000 to under $1 million.

Personal representative and attorney compensation is capped at 9% of the first $20,000 plus 3.6% of the value above $20,000, though an attorney can petition for more for good cause. Funeral expenses up to $15,000 can be paid without a court order when the estate is solvent and the will allows it. A surviving spouse or registered domestic partner receives a $10,000 family allowance, and each unmarried minor child receives $5,000.

Maryland's inheritance tax has a 10% collateral rate for recipients outside the exempt groups, which include spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings and their lineal descendants. The first $1,000 passing to any one person is exempt.

Selling an inherited house quickly

Heirs usually face a gap between wanting to sell and having legal authority to do so. Until a personal representative is appointed, nobody holds the powers that Estates and Trusts § 7-401 describes.

Selling as-is to a cash buyer can take repairs off the family's list, but the personal representative still has to follow the notice and claims calendar above. Before closing, gather the Letters, the death certificate and any bond paperwork in one folder. The title company will ask for them, and having them ready keeps the closing date from slipping.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does probate take in Maryland?

A regular estate follows a schedule of about nine months to the first account, and a modified administration is designed to close in about 13 months. Contested or complicated estates run longer.

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Maryland?

Generally yes, if the house was in the decedent's sole name. The personal representative's authority begins when Letters of Administration are issued, and the Register issues them after the petition is processed.

Can the personal representative sell the house without asking the court?

Usually. Estates and Trusts § 7-401 lets a personal representative sell estate property without court approval unless the will limits that power.

What is a small estate in Maryland?

It is an estate with probate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less when the surviving spouse is the sole heir or legatee. There is no filing fee, and no inheritance tax is collected on probate property.

Does Maryland charge an inheritance tax?

Yes, on certain recipients. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents and siblings are exempt, and the collateral rate is 10% for others, with the first $1,000 to any one person exempt.

Maryland tax on a house sale

Most Marylanders pay no special capital gains rate. Profit on a house lands in your income, gets the normal state brackets, and picks up local income tax. A new 2% add-on applies starting with tax year 2025 to net capital gains of anyone with federal adjusted gross income over $350,000.

The add-on is stacked on the regular tax, so a seller over the line pays both. Corporations are exempt from it. A pass-through entity does not pay it, though an owner who receives gain from one can, and a trust or estate with federal taxable income over $350,000 owes it on undistributed gains.

Most homeowners who sell a primary residence never meet the surtax, because that gain is excluded when the sale price stays under a set limit. The next section explains it.

Sales excluded from the extra 2%

A primary residence that sells for less than $1.5 million is excluded from the 2% surtax. Covered property types are a single-family home, townhome, row home, or a residential condo or co-op unit, including the land and any accessory dwelling unit.

Other exclusions matter less to a house seller:

  • Gain held in retirement accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA.
  • Land under a conservation, agricultural or forest preservation easement.
  • Gain deferred in a like-kind exchange under IRC section 1031, since it is outside federal AGI.
  • Affordable housing owned by a nonprofit.

A rental house, a second home or an inherited house you never lived in is not a primary residence. For a seller above the $350,000 line, gain on any of those can be hit by the extra 2%.

State and local income tax rates

For tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, Maryland's top brackets are 5.75%, 6.25% and 6.5%, depending on income. The lowest bracket starts at 2% on the first $1,000. Counties and Baltimore City add their own local income tax.

State rateSingle filersJoint filers and heads of household
5.75%$250,001 to $500,000$300,001 to $600,000
6.25%$500,001 to $1,000,000$600,001 to $1,200,000
6.50%Over $1,000,000Over $1,200,000

Counties may charge up to 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County charges 3.06% and Howard County 3.20% for calendar 2026.

A large house gain counts as income, so it can push the year's total into a higher bracket. A tax professional can run the numbers on your own return.

The federal home sale exclusion

Federal law lets a homeowner shield $250,000 of profit from the sale of a main home, or $500,000 for a married couple filing together. Two tests apply. Within the 5 years before closing, you must have owned the house for 24 months and also lived in it for 24 months.

The two tests do not have to overlap. One 2-year stretch can satisfy ownership and another can satisfy use. A second exclusion within 2 years of an earlier one is generally off the table.

A reduced exclusion may be available when the sale is driven by a work change, a health problem or an unforeseeable event such as a death, a divorce or a home destroyed by disaster. The formula divides your qualifying time by 730 days and multiplies by $250,000. You must report the sale on Schedule D and Form 8949 if a Form 1099-S arrives or if part of the gain is taxable.

Federal rates on gain above the exclusion

If you owned the home longer than a year, profit beyond the exclusion is taxed at one of three federal rates (0%, 15% or 20%) set by your income. The 2025 breakpoints:

  • 0% up to $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • 15% above that, up to $533,400 for single filers, $600,050 for joint filers and $566,700 for heads of household.
  • 20% above the 15% range.

A house held a year or less produces short-term gain, taxed like wages. Depreciation recapture on real property (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) can be taxed at up to 25%.

A 3.8% net investment income tax may also apply once income passes $200,000 (single or head of household) or $250,000 (joint). Gain you exclude on a principal residence generally escapes it. Gain above the exclusion can count toward it.

How to work out your gain

Subtract your adjusted basis from the amount realized and you have the gain. The amount realized is the sale price minus what it cost to sell. Your basis is the purchase price plus buying costs, increased by improvements that add value.

Closing costs you pay as seller reduce the amount realized, so they work in your favor. File away the final settlement statement, the closing disclosure from your purchase and improvement receipts. If the IRS or the Comptroller questions your basis, those papers answer.

Inherited houses use a different starting point: fair market value at the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate picked one. Where an estate tax return was filed or required, use the value reported there.

Rental or business use calls for care. Depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 is taxable as unrecaptured section 1250 gain whatever the exclusion. Years after 2008 when the house was not your principal residence are generally nonqualified use, and the gain tied to those years is not excludable.

Nonresident sellers and withholding at closing

A nonresident selling Maryland real property has tax withheld at settlement: 8.75% of the total payment for individuals and 8.25% for entities, on sales after June 30, 2025. The deed cannot be recorded unless the withholding payment comes with it.

Form MW506NRS reports the withholding. A seller who owes less than the amount withheld, or nothing, may request an early refund if the price is under $1.5 million. At $1.5 million or more, no tentative refund is available and the seller files a full annual return, with Form 502CG where it applies. Form MW506AE is the application for a certificate of full or partial exemption.

The withholding leaves out the extra 2% surtax. A seller who expects to owe it should make additional estimated payments with Form 502D.

Does a cash buyer change the tax?

No. Maryland and federal tax on your gain turn on your basis, holding period and income. They do not depend on who buys the house or how the buyer pays. With a cash buyer, the price you realize is simply the price in the contract.

What a fast cash sale changes is timing. Hoping to claim the home sale exclusion? Run the 24-month tests against your planned closing date before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Does Maryland tax profit on a home sale?

Yes, as ordinary income plus local tax. An added 2% surtax hits net capital gains once federal adjusted gross income passes $350,000, and a primary residence sold under $1.5 million is left out of it.

How much profit can I exclude federally?

$250,000 if single, $500,000 if filing jointly, provided you owned and lived in the house for 24 months during the last 5 years.

Do Maryland counties add tax to my capital gain?

Yes, through the local income tax, which is capped at 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County charges 3.06% and Howard County 3.20%.

What if I live elsewhere and sell here?

Settlement withholds 8.75% for an individual and 8.25% for an entity. Under $1.5 million you can ask for a refund of any excess, and at or above it you file a full annual return.

What basis do I get on an inherited house?

Usually its value on the date of death (or the estate's alternate valuation date). A required or filed estate tax return fixes that value.

What happens at a Maryland tax sale?

The county sells a lien, not the house. A buyer at the auction pays the overdue tax bill and receives a tax lien certificate, and the homeowner keeps ownership and possession while the debt is outstanding.

Property taxes are due July 1 and overdue October 1. Principal residences can pay in two installments, due September 30 and December 31. A collector must mail a notice at least 30 days before newspaper advertising starts, and the sale is advertised weekly for four weeks.

About six months after the sale, the purchaser receives a certificate of sale, and it is void if no foreclosure case is filed within two years. Counties run their own sales, so dates and minimum amounts differ. Baltimore City, for instance, follows a notice calendar that runs from a February final bill to a sale in the third week of May, with payment due April 30 to stop it.

  • Sold: the lien, through a tax lien certificate.
  • Not sold: the title to the house.
  • Owner keeps: possession and the right to redeem until a court forecloses.

Tax sale activity in 2024

In 2024, counties mailed final bill and legal notices to 77,050 properties statewide, and 16,205 liens were offered for sale. Most owners who get a notice resolve it before the auction. The numbers below cover tax sales held in 2024 and redemptions and foreclosures in fiscal year 2024, reported by every county and Baltimore City.

The ombudsman assisted about 10,116 homeowners in fiscal year 2025 and more than 20,000 since 2020. The gap between 13,669 advertised parcels and 81 foreclosures shows how many owners pay, redeem or get help along the way.

Rule changes effective January 1, 2026

Chapter 231 of the 2025 laws (House Bill 59) tightened tax sale rules for owner-occupied homes, effective January 1, 2026. It applies only to tax sale certificates issued after that date.

  • A home occupied by an heir of a deceased owner is treated like an owner-occupied home, and local governments may withhold it from sale.
  • The mandatory withholding threshold for owner-occupied and heir-occupied homes rises from $750 to $1,000.
  • A property must be withheld when the only tax lien is for unpaid water and sewer charges, statewide.
  • The redemption rate for owner-occupied residential property can't exceed 10 percent per year.
  • Post-sale taxes, interest and penalties can't be added to the redemption price for owner-occupied homes.
  • Foreclosure complaints on owner-occupied homes can be filed after 12 months instead of 9, and the first required notice can't go out until 10 months after the sale.

The law also makes counties and Baltimore City set up a registry where interested parties, or the State Tax Sale Ombudsman, can designate properties to be withheld.

Redemption and what it costs

The owner pays the certificate holder what is owed and the lien is cleared. The total includes the original tax debt, interest at the rate on the certificate, and allowed fees, and it grows the longer the owner waits.

Interest runs from 6 percent to 18 percent a year depending on the county. Anne Arundel County charges 1.5 percent a month, or 18 percent a year, and Baltimore County charges 12 percent a year. For owner-occupied homes on certificates issued under the 2026 rules, the cap is 10 percent.

An owner can redeem any time until a court finally forecloses the right of redemption. Some purchaser fees become recoverable after four months, so redeeming in the early weeks costs less. Ask the Collector of Taxes for the redemption amount in writing, and redeem before final judgment, because paying afterward doesn't restore your rights.

Foreclosing the right of redemption

The certificate holder must file a case in circuit court after a waiting period, and the owner is entitled to written notice first. If the court enters a final judgment, the holder takes title free of earlier encumbrances other than later taxes and easements.

The waiting period before filing has been six months in most counties and nine months for owner-occupied homes. Two notices go out: a pre-foreclosure notice and then a notice of intent sent at least 30 days before the complaint. The holder has to prove both were sent.

Tenants in a foreclosed rental house are covered too. Under the 2025 law, a tenant must get at least 90 days' notice before the plaintiff takes possession, up from 30, and notices must be posted on the property within 5 days instead of 1. Foreclosure plaintiffs on owner-occupied property must also notify the State Tax Sale Ombudsman.

Help for owners facing a tax sale

Maryland offers a state loan program, income-based tax credits and a free help center. Use them early, since options narrow after the sale.

  • Homeowner Protection Program: may keep an eligible home out of tax sale for at least 3 years. Limits are an assessed value of $300,000 or less, combined income of $60,000 or less, and non-property assets of $200,000 or less, with priority for owners over 60, people on disability benefits and long-time residents.
  • Homeowners' Property Tax Credit: income based, reapplied for yearly, with a September 1 application deadline.
  • Homestead Tax Credit: caps yearly taxable assessment increases and needs a one-time application.
  • Tax Sale Help Center: by appointment at 123 Market Place in Baltimore; call (410) 767-4994 or email sdat.taxsale@maryland.gov.

If court papers arrive, contact the Legal Aid Bureau or the Maryland Volunteer Lawyers Service.

Selling before the tax sale

You can. Because the owner still holds title until a court says otherwise, a house with a tax lien can be sold, and the unpaid taxes are paid out of the closing proceeds.

Real Property Article 3-104 requires the county collector's certificate showing taxes and charges paid before a deed is recorded, so the debt can't be skipped at closing. Selling before the auction avoids certificate interest, foreclosure risk and the costs that may be added to a redemption.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including houses behind on property taxes or carrying other liens. If you have a final bill or sale notice, call the collector first for the exact payoff, then compare options with the sale deadline in mind.

Counties also hold bid balance funds, with Baltimore City holding the most at $8,783,544, Prince George's County $8,488,803 and Montgomery County $6,519,562. Ask the county collector what applies to a specific property.

Frequently asked questions

Do I lose my house at a Maryland tax sale?

No, not at the sale. The county sells a tax lien certificate and the homeowner keeps the property. The owner can lose it only if the certificate holder forecloses the right of redemption and a court enters final judgment.

How long do I have to redeem after a Maryland tax sale?

Until a court finally forecloses the right of redemption. Waiting periods before a foreclosure case can be filed run from six months upward, and 12 months for owner-occupied homes under certificates issued from 2026.

What interest do I pay to redeem?

The rate on the certificate, which runs 6 to 18 percent a year by county. For owner-occupied homes under the 2026 law it can't exceed 10 percent.

When are Maryland property taxes overdue?

October 1. They are due July 1, and principal residences may pay in two installments on September 30 and December 31.

Can a home occupied by an heir be sold at tax sale?

Under Chapter 231 of 2025, an heir-occupied residence is treated like an owner-occupied home. Local governments may withhold it from sale, and it must be withheld when taxes owed are under the mandatory threshold.

The state transfer tax rate

The state transfer tax is 0.5% of the consideration on the deed, set by Tax-Property Article section 13-203. It is charged before any local taxes.

Consideration includes any mortgage or deed of trust the buyer takes over. It leaves out debt that was forgiven or that no longer secures the property.

A lower rate of 0.25% applies when the buyer is a first-time Maryland home buyer who will live in the house as a principal residence. The seller pays that reduced tax entirely. Maryland defines a first-time buyer as someone who has never owned Maryland residential property that was their principal residence.

Who pays transfer tax and recordation tax at closing

Unless the contract or another law says otherwise, Maryland presumes the buyer and seller split recordation tax and any state or local transfer tax equally. Real Property section 14-104 sets that default, and it doesn't apply to mortgages or deeds of trust.

The default flips when a first-time buyer is involved. For improved residential property bought as a principal residence, the seller pays all of the state transfer tax. The seller also pays the recordation tax and local transfer tax, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise. The state portion can't be shifted by agreement.

Three conditions come with that rule:

  • Each buyer, or the buyer's agent, signs a statement under oath that the buyer is a first-time buyer who will occupy the home. A non-occupying co-signer on the purchase loan can sign a matching statement.
  • With several buyers, the rule applies only if every one of them qualifies in one of those two ways.
  • The rule doesn't apply to tax sales under Title 14, Subtitle 8 of the Tax-Property Article.

Contracts for homes with one or two units must also carry a conspicuous statement that these taxes are shared equally unless negotiated otherwise. That requirement appears in section 14-117, which also covers other notices Maryland sellers owe buyers, including a homestead tax credit statement on every residential sale.

Why the total bill changes by county

The state rate stays the same everywhere, and counties add their own recordation and transfer taxes on top. The FY 2026 local rate table shows these examples:

Counties and Baltimore City also have the option to exempt part or all of the recordation tax for owner-occupied homes bought by first-time buyers or by buyers who occupy the home for at least 7 months of a 12-month period. Whether a county has used those options is a local question, so call its land records office before assuming a figure.

Transfers exempt from state transfer tax

State transfer tax is waived for transfers that are also exempt from recordation tax, plus a few extras. Section 13-207 and the recordation exemptions in section 12-108 together cover a long list. The ones home sellers run into most often:

  • Transfers between spouses, or between domestic partners
  • Transfers from an estate, which matters for inherited houses
  • Certain transfers into or out of a trust
  • Transfers to or from the federal, state or local government
  • Court judgments and orders of satisfaction
  • A principal residence surrendered in bankruptcy to the holder of its purchase money mortgage, under set conditions
  • Deeds that carry out a prior contract of sale where tax was already paid
  • Leases of 7 years or less

Each exemption has conditions. A deed that claims one has to name which one, and Prince George's County, for example, asks that exemption deeds cite every applicable code section from the Annotated Code.

Where the state transfer tax money goes

Most of it funds land conservation and parks. After the cost of administering the tax is deducted, the remaining revenue goes into a special fund, and section 13-209 splits the balance. Program Open Space gets 75.15%, plus 1% for land acquisition. The Agricultural Land Preservation Fund gets 17.05%, the Rural Legacy Program 5%, and the Heritage Conservation Fund 1.8%.

For fiscal years 2026 through 2029, $25 million is moved to the General Fund first, and the program shares shrink proportionally. Revenue is first pledged to any outstanding bonds that rely on it.

Agricultural transfer tax on a house sale

The agricultural transfer tax is a separate charge that applies when land with a farm-use assessment is sold. It is easy to miss if a rural Maryland house sits on acreage that was once assessed as farmland.

  • The tax is 5% for 20 acres or more, 4% for under 20 acres, and 3% for under 20 acres with site improvements such as a well and septic.
  • A 25% surcharge is added, though it doesn't apply to transfers of two acres or less to a child or grandchild of the owner.
  • The tax falls on the deed, so who pays is negotiable. The seller has to tell the buyer in writing in the sales contract that it may be due, and after that notice the buyer carries it.
  • A buyer can file a Declaration of Intent to farm the land for at least five full consecutive taxable years, which waives the tax.
  • The tax must be paid before the deed can be recorded, and the assessment office should hear about new improvements at least 7 days before recording.
